Lot essay:

“I will run with the painting, like it’s a dog on a leash, chasing and almost falling behind it. That is also the space where I forget myself, where painting becomes something that I don’t control, neither emotionally nor intellectually” - Charline von Heyl (J. Farago, “An Interview with Charline von Heyl”, Even Magazine, no. 7, 2017, online).

Charline von Heyl’s painting practice occupies a crucial place in contemporary art for its rigorous investigation of what painting can be and do in the twenty-first century. Eschewing both pure abstraction and traditional figuration, von Heyl creates works that resist easy categorization. Her paintings unfold as nuanced visual events—layered, contradictory, and dynamic—challenging viewers to experience rather than interpret them. This resistance to fixity is central to her practice: von Heyl redefines painting as a process of continuous becoming rather than a static image.

A distinctive feature of von Heyl’s oeuvre is her steadfast engagement with the history of painting while refusing nostalgia. She draws upon the legacies of Cubism, Pop, Abstract Expressionism, and Op Art, yet transforms these influences into something distinctly her own. Her surfaces often contain traces of erasure, overpainting, and disruption, revealing the tension between intention and accident. In doing so, von Heyl exposes the act of painting as a form of thinking—an active dialogue between intuition, intellect, and the materiality of the work itself.

Von Heyl’s practice also expands the possibilities of abstraction. Rather than treating abstraction as a language of purity or transcendence, she treats it as a site of play, contradiction, and psychological charge. Her images—at once seductive and disorienting—invite viewers to navigate multiple registers of visual and emotional experience. This sense of instability and openness mirrors contemporary life, making her work both timely and timeless.

Ultimately, Charline von Heyl’s practice lies in her refusal to allow painting to settle into complacency. She reaffirms painting’s capacity to surprise, to question perception, and to sustain complexity in an age dominated by instant images and digital proliferation. Her work demonstrates that painting, far from obsolete, remains one of the most vital forms of critical and imaginative inquiry.

Lot essay:

“Color as an object is earthly material stuff. Color as subject arches over everything like a rainbow, from cosmic rays to the minerals in the earth to what happens inside your eyes, from religious symbology to philosophical problems, from phenomena to noumena. But aside from all that, color is just the tool that a painter wields in making a painting. To deal with color as a painter is to render these overarching problems as physical propositions, as sensuous experiences synesthetically merged under the sign of the hand.” - Amy Sillman

Amy Sillman’s paintings occupy a vibrant space between abstraction and figuration, where color and gesture become tools for exploring emotion, thought, and perception. Her abstraction resists purity; instead, it embraces awkwardness, revision, and contradiction. Sillman builds and reworks her compositions through layers of paint, allowing traces of earlier decisions to remain visible, creating a sense of both movement and psychological depth.

Color in Sillman’s work is both expressive and disruptive, as shown in the present lot Untitled, which the artist completed in 2014. She juxtaposes muted tones with jolts of saturated hues—acidic greens against dusky purples or fleshy pinks beside gray tonalities—to evoke tension and surprise. These unexpected combinations challenge harmony and instead convey the complexity and nuance of feeling. Her color acts as a form of inquiry, exposing the instability of visual and emotional experience.

Through this dynamic interplay of color, form, and gesture, Sillman redefines abstraction as a deeply human practice—intellectual, humorous, and profoundly affective.

Lot note: 
Due to declining physical strength, Joseph Cornell, in his late fifties, moved away from creating three-dimensional shadow box constructions to working exclusively in collage on board. The collages allowed him to continue exploring visually intriguing juxtapositions. 

The typed written text on the reverse was clipped by the artist from Scientific American, vol. 204, January 1, 1961, p. 134 from an article by T. H. Benzinger.

The full text read as: THE HUMAN THERMOSTAT. A newly discovered sensory organ in the brain precisely measures the body temperature and trips the heat-dissipating mechanisms that maintain the temperature within a fraction of one degree.

Joseph Cornell covered the three words, “in the brain” with an aviary stamp and used the resultant quotation of text as a playful explanation for his collage cut-out in the verso image. Bird images and travel were constant themes in Cornell’s box constructions and collages.

Exhibited:
New York, New York, DC Moore Gallery, Jacob Lawrence Paintings, Drawings and Prints from 1937-1998, December 12, 2001-January 26, 2002

Best recognized for his masterfully flat stylized modernist depictions of the African American experience, Jacob Lawrence (American, 1917-2000) is universally celebrated as one of the most important African American artists and expressive cultural voices of the 20th century. Lawrence came of age in New York’s Harlem of the Great Depression, where, as a beneficiary of the artistic renaissance in the decade prior, he cut his artistic teeth in the WPA Easel Division and Harlem Art Workshop and developed his unique socially conscious narrative painting approach. Working in his favored tempera paint or kindred gouache, Lawrence took inspiration from the limitation of the fast-drying, opaque media to employ what he referred to as “dynamic cubism”: arranging bold flat passages of color in collage-like fashion, dramatically layering the shapes and characters to intentionally distort and foreshorten the perspective on the stage of the picture plane. In his highly heralded paintings, Lawrence remarkably visually simplifies various existential complexities to the essential, arrestingly and impactfully documenting the breadth of the accomplishments and the struggles of black people in America. 
 
Painted in 1953, a significant decade in the artist’s oeuvre, the presently offered gouache Time demonstrates an established and mature artist operating at his peak painterly prowess. The work is composed of an arrangement that first appears static and nonobjective, of unmodulated and sophistically colored shapes, but as eyes adjust the dynamism of the scene slowly vibrates: a solitary figure hunched over a desk or table—
perhaps at work, possibly sleeping, maybe in despair—with a partial realized alarm clock adjacently ticking. As if out of the subject’s imagination or dream, stark, stylized branches punctuated by colorful leaves and blossoms surround in a cyclical network of naturalistic geometry, both symbolic of seasonal progression and art historically evocative of the sculptural movement of contemporary Calder mobiles. Rendered in lushly matte gouache, the material itself echoing the lucid dreamlike contemplative feel of the work with its soft yet no less richly saturated pigmentation. We see fabric folds in candy reds, pinks and teals, the crisp coffee black slouched shoulder and hung head of the main character outlined and highlighted in chalky chocolate brown, an entangled system of twigs, stems, petals and fronds vibrant blooms of primary hues, the stoic blue of the clock face with decisive numerals, and the autumnal yellows and ochers of the backing wall awash with dancing structural and spectral shadows.
 
Lawrence confidentially leans into the language of abstraction more than one might expect, aptly addressing the ethereal conceptual abstract of time in this painting, while still staying tethered to the representational ground of his hallmark Humanism. The artist tellingly stated, “The Human subject is the most important thing. My work is abstract in the sense of having been designed and composed, but it is not abstract in the sense of having no human content I want to communicate. I want the idea to strike right away.” In Time the idea sure does strike, like the ring of the daily alarm clock and the ultimate toll of the bell that in many ways defines what it is to be human and mortal. Amplifying the philosophical headiness of the painting is the self-conscious enigmatic quality, accentuated by the furtive body language of the central figure and the strange, layered patterning of the enveloping foliage. It is the ambiguity of the human circumstance represented that makes the work so alive, at once compellingly intriguing and relatably accessible, evergreen in concept and content. As viewers, we are captivated, not just unable to look away, but fully sucked into the forward marching allegory of the powerful pressure and influence the sands of time have on us all, transfixed by the ticking hands of the clock hoping to discover just what time it is right now. Something is happening here in this seemingly simple fleeting moment captured, something both personal and transcendent, something inescapably human as signified by the reality and existential awareness of numbered days. The inherent power of the work, beyond the obvious and objective aesthetic merits, is that Lawrence translates his deep and sensitive understanding of humanity by displaying that everyday mysteries are just as mysterious as the timeless variety.

Lot essay:

“I like my women to be presented as very conscientious, very empowered, very charismatic – strong women who are aware of their environment and their experiences. I’m not making them do anything. It’s a collaborative effort because I’m taking the image, I’m photographing them, but they’re aware of me doing this with them. It’s not as though the artist is explaining the sitter.” - Mickalene Thomas 

Mickalene Thomas’ portraiture has had a transformative impact on contemporary art history by redefining how Black women are represented and celebrated in visual culture at large. Drawing from art history, pop culture, and personal narrative, Thomas fuses elements of painting, collage, photography, and rhinestone embellishment to create images that radiate confidence, sensuality, and power. Indeed, her portraits challenge the Eurocentric canon by reimagining classical poses and compositions through a distinctly Black, female lens. In doing so, Thomas not only inserts Black women into the history of art but also reframes beauty, glamour, and identity as sites of self-definition rather than external judgment. Her work has reshaped conversations about representation and visibility, asserting that portraiture can be both a political act and a deeply personal affirmation of presence and pride.

Thomas' work is included in myriad private and public collections in the United States and worldwide, including The Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney Museum of American Art, The Art Institute of Chicago, and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum. A significant mid-career international retrospective was recently assembled for the artist, entitled All About Love, which explores themes of Black womanhood, identity, and empowerment through a multidisciplinary lens. The exhibition showcases over 90 works spanning two decades of Thomas' career, including paintings, collages, photographs, and installations. Co-organized by the Hayward Gallery, London, The Broad, Los Angeles, in partnership with the Barnes Foundation in Philadelphia and Les Abattoirs – Musée-Frac Occitanie Toulouse, the exhibition firmly underscores Thomas as one of the most relevant artists living today.

Exhibited:
New York, New York, Cordier & Ekstrom, Fritz Scholder, January 8 - February 9, 1974

Fritz Scholder (Luiseño, 1937-2005) pushed boundaries and critically challenged existing traditions, working to shift Native American art from an overly idealized category plucked from nineteenth-century stereotypes to a thriving part of the contemporary art world. His paintings defy classification—transcending the categories of traditional, modern, Pop, Indian, not Indian—and continue to provoke intrigue through these contradictions. This is clear in Insane Indian no. 25, where a Native American illustrated in Pop aesthetics undermines preexisting expectations and is thus able to attain a greater degree of his own agency.

Scholder, of part Native American and part European ancestry, often said he was "not Indian" in the traditional sense, which gave him a unique, often controversial lens on Native identity. Inspired by his own experiences, he began painting Native Americans in ways that directly confronted and shattered long-standing depictions. As he explained, ‘“I vowed to myself that I would not paint Indians. Then I saw the numerous over-romanticized paintings of the ‘noble savage’ . . . and decided that someone should paint the Indian in a different context.” Rather than stoic warriors or mystical figures, his subjects were modern, complex, and often subversive: Native Americans awash in bright colors drinking beer, smoking cigarettes, eating ice cream cones, or draped in the American flag.

Insane Indian no. 25 (1972) illustrates a man in three quarter profile on a deep red ground balanced in simplified geometry. The composition emphasizes solidity—the man’s oval head, predominately in black, with white nose, feather, and highlights, mirrors the white arch of his chest. The alternating blacks and whites that define his chest and shoulders grounds his head, while accents of red, green, and peach weave through the figure in increasingly abstracted strokes. The title Insane Indian confuses.

The American West’s mythology of its relationship to indigenous cultures might anticipate an ‘insane Indian’ more in the realm of a berserker, a fierce opponent, a foil. Yet, Scholder’s depiction is the picture of equanimity. The expected cultural connotation is denied by the man’s apparent stability. Should the man be disturbed or in some way distressed, it is internal. But, his eyes, defined only in abstract swipes, negate a means for the viewer to truly interrogate this internality. The man’s complex inner life remains his alone, afforded a greater capacity of emotional depth than the Native American of American fiction.

This provocative painting by Scholder thus reflects the heart of his practice of depicting indigenous culture. While including some traditional trappings in some ways expected of Native Americans in painting such as feathered garments, Scholder digs deeper, resulting in a quiet yet captivating portrait of a man’s emotional life.

In Portrait of Al Held (1963), Alex Katz (American, b. 1927) balances familiarity and objectivity through his signature painting style and direct composition in order to create a striking portrait of his long-time friend and fellow artist Al Held (American, 1928-2005).

The subject of more than 200 solo exhibitions and international acclaim, Alex Katz applies a deliberately vibrant visual language between realism and abstraction, ambivalence and intimacy. Coming of age alongside the titans of New York’s Abstract Expressionism of the 1950s, Katz favored flatness of color and form rather than gestural primacy and raw emotion. His work is deceptively simple; his technique of painting wet on wet evokes a lustrous finish to his canvases, defying two-dimensionality even in their flatness. 

In terms of his thematic output, Katz is particular known for sharing his world, whether through hundreds of portraits of his wife of more than 60 years, Ada, his home in coastal Maine, or scenes and characters from downtown New York City among the cultural avant garde. This combination of immediacy and familiarity— flash-in-the-pan moments he captures in thick brushstrokes and meditatively stylized forms is clear in his depiction of Held.

Katz and Held met during in New York during the mid-century, when they were each in their 20s. For a time, both artists had studios in the same building, and saw each other’s work often. Katz has said of Held’s paintings then that “I think Al did some of the best artwork
on the planet at that time and I was very lucky to be near them.”[i] But, while Held focused primarily on abstraction, Katz continued to find the most meaning in figuration.

As Katz has said:
"Realist painting has to do with leaving out a lot of detail,” said Katz in an interview, “I think my painting can be a little shocking in all that it leaves out. But what happens is that the mind fills in what's missing. It's about being able to see something in a specific way. Painting is a way of making you see what I saw."[ii]
In this 1963 painting, Held, defined in surprisingly simplified forms in blues, browns, yellows, and whites. Without any tools of his trade, his blue-collared shirt, combed back hair, and direct eye contact, Katz illustrates Held not as a fellow artist but as an austere, stripped-back portrait of someone he knew well.

[i] Juan Manuel Bonet, “Alex Katz: A Great Figurative Voice,” Electra, Issue 17, 2022. https://electramagazine.fundacaoedp.pt/en/editions/issue-17/alex-katz-great-figurative-voice.
[ii] Aida Dunne, “I prefer Stan Getz to Sartre”, The Irish Times, March 3, 2007. https://www.irishtimes.com/news/i-prefer-stan-getz-to-sartre-1.1198117.

Exhibited:
Chicago, The Chicago No-Jury Society of Artists, Twelfth Annual Exhibition, June 13 - June 27, 1936, no. 1
Chicago, The Chicago Society of Artists 50th Exhibition, April 1939, no. 2
New York, Karma, Gertrude Abercrombie, August 9-September 23, 2018, p. 127, illus.

At the time the present portrait was executed, in 1936, Gertrude Abercrombie had been working on the New Deal government art projects for almost two years, initially for the Public Works of Art Project, followed in 1935 by the Illinois Art Project (IAP) of the Works Progress Administration (WPA). In contrast to Abercrombie’s later work, which is often small in scale and painted on Masonite panels, the works made for the project were paintings on canvas of a standard size, ranging from 24 x 20 inches to 30 x 40 inches. The WPA required one painting a month from each artist employed on the easel painting project, which left most artists with quite a bit of free time to produce other work. As Abercrombie was used to the format mandated by the projects, her independent work tended to be on canvas and of this size. She continued to paint on this scale, at least some of the time, into the mid 1940s.   

Abercrombie’s appointment to the PWAP and its regular monthly paycheck not only gave her the imprimatur of a legitimate artist, but it also allowed her to move out of her parents’ home and into an apartment of her own in the Weinstein Building in Hyde Park, which was home to many artists and writers. It was there that she met lifelong friends and made many connections with other artists and writers. Like many artists in the early stages of their careers, Abercrombie’s early work includes many portraits, both of herself and of these new friends and colleagues, who were willing subjects and offered her the opportunity to hone her skills. Her earliest work includes portraits of artists Tud Kempf, Macena Barton, Rudolph Weisenborn, Franklin Van Court Brown, Charles Sebree, and John Pratt. She also painted writer friends such as Thornton Wilder, Gertrude Stein, Wendell Wilcox, and James Purdy. Other portraits from this early period include art world figures like Cati Mount, Helen Mann, Inez Cunningham Stark, actors Grace Cornell and Davis Roberts, as well as family members Laura and Maurine Campbell and Elinor Porter Carlberg. This not only attests to the varied and noteworthy social connections she established in the first decade of her career, but from the beginning her portraits were distinctive, penetrating, and often idiosyncratic, usually offering an extremely intimate image of the sitter. Almost all of them include just the head or a small portion of the upper body of the sitter, sometimes with a disconnected arm or hand (see Thornton Wilder, for example, whose chin rests on a hand that emerges from the bottom of the painting and could be an inanimate object) which often have expressive purposes.   

By 1936, Edward (Eddie) Millman was already a well-established presence in the art world of Chicago. The year after designing murals for the 1933 Century of Progress World’s Fair, he traveled to Mexico to study with Diego Rivera. Upon his return, he became one of the most productive artists on the government supported projects, creating both easel paintings for the Illinois Art Project and murals for the competitive national Treasury Section for Painting and Sculpture. By the time Abercrombie painted his portrait, Millman had executed murals for the post offices in Moline (1935) and Decatur (1936). It’s possible that they became acquainted through their work on the IAP, or through other artist friends.   

While the present portrait is like that of other art world friends or acquaintances of Abercrombie’s, it is likely the only portrait image that includes the sitter’s entire body, in this case literally from head to foot. And while Eddie Millman’s entire form is visible, it is distorted in a way that may reveal several things: Abercrombie’s own difficulty with the human form; an effort to experiment with modernist distortion; and her interest in conveying something more than a strict likeness in her portrait. Although she excelled at the traditional techniques of chiaroscuro and perspective, which she learned through numerous art classes, she struggled with the human form. The artist avoids the complexities of anatomical accuracy in the many later paintings where she represents herself in a landscape or interior scene, by developing a simplified flattened form. In this painting, Millman seemingly sits sideways, his left arm draped over the back of the chair, his left leg crossed over his right. Abercrombie’s difficulty with creating a lap for the figure makes it look almost as if the upper body and the lower body have been pieced together without a midsection. This may also point to her interest in experimenting with modernist modes. This can be seen in her attempt to incorporate an avantgarde style in other work of the time, such as Self Portrait with Cat (She and I), c. 1934 in which she introduces an angularity reminiscent of Cubism; Nude with Guitar, c. 1934, an experiment in creating a full length nude; and her Self Portrait in Green, 1938 (Illinois State Museum), in which the large three quarter length figure shows some familiarity with a post-Cubist Picasso. Abercrombie, despite developing a recognizable mature style, had a curiosity that drove her to explore different modes of expression throughout her career. This may be another example of that experimentation. 

But the real achievement in the Portrait of Eddie Millman is in the creation of a figure who is complex, his body an abstracted combination of shapes, while his face displays a direct, open, honest gaze, that of a man with whom the viewer can connect. Whether intentional or not, the distortions of his body contrast with his straightforward countenance to project the competent, intelligent artist as a multifaceted, modern, complicated individual. and Portrait of Eddie Millman is an exceptional example of Abercrombie’s early proficiency to reveal multiple, even conflicting, ideas in the same work.

Note:
Thomas Chimes’s career was marked by certain specific artistic stages of exploration: the Crucifixion Paintings, Metal Boxes, Panel Portraits and White Paintings. In 1979, Chimes stood at the transition between two of these periods, finished with the series of panel portraits, and experiencing an artistic crisis of what would follow. A personal crossroads was taking place simultaneously, as the year marked a painful period in his life, with his separation from his wife. During this difficult time, Chimes moved his studio to the former studio of fellow Philadelphia artist Tommy Dale Palmore, who had hung a large gessoed canvas up over the windows to control the light and view from the street. Chimes fell in love with the buttery, layered surface and purchased the canvas from Palmore when he moved in, drawing renewed inspiration from its open possibilities.

Moving away from the intricate detail of his panel portraits, Chimes returned to the painted surface, as he had previously explored in his Crucifixion series, while also trying to work more immediately and spontaneously. He painted his first large canvas quickly all over with an aquamarine blue, which became the basis for his first Waterfall painting. Reflecting on a happier time in his marriage when the couple had visited Niagara Falls, as well as art historical precedents in Albert Bierstadt, Thomas Moran, John Henry Twachtman and Joseph Mallord William Turner, the waterfall became a place to delve into ethereal, natural beauty, as well as contemplate the transitions happening in his life. The present lot is one of few examples of the Chimes’s luminous Waterfall, representing this crucial shift in the artist’s life and career.
